\"Southern Sami language\"): *Tråante*), historically **Kaupangen**, **[Nidaros](./Nidaros \"Nidaros\")**, and **Trondhjem** (locally [[ˈtrɔ̂nːjæm]](./Help:IPA \"Help:IPA\") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:Trondheim.ogg \"File:Trondheim.ogg\")), is a city and [municipality](./List_of_municipalities_of_Norway \"List of municipalities of Norway\") in [Trøndelag](./Trøndelag \"Trøndelag\") county, [Norway](./Norway \"Norway\"). As of 2025, it had a population of 216,518.[[8]](./Trondheim#cite_note-8) Trondheim is the third most populous municipality in Norway, and is the [fourth largest](./List_of_continuously_built-up_areas_in_Norway_by_population \"List of continuously built-up areas in Norway by population\") [urban area](./Urban_area \"Urban area\"). Trondheim lies on the south shore of [Trondheim Fjord](./Trondheim_Fjord \"Trondheim Fjord\") at the mouth of the River [Nidelva](./Nidelva \"Nidelva\"). Among the significant technology-oriented institutions headquartered in Trondheim are the [Norwegian University of Science and Technology](./Norwegian_University_of_Science_and_Technology \"Norwegian University of Science and Technology\") (NTNU), the [Foundation for Scientific and Industrial Research (SINTEF)](./SINTEF \"SINTEF\"), the [Geological Survey of Norway](./Geological_Survey_of_Norway \"Geological Survey of Norway\") (NGU), and [St. Olavs University Hospital](./St._Olavs_University_Hospital \"St. Olavs University Hospital\").\\n\\nThe settlement was founded in 997 as a trading post and served as the capital of Norway through the [Viking Age](./Viking_Age \"Viking Age\") until 1217. From 1152 to 1537, the city was the seat of the Catholic [Archdiocese of Nidaros](./Archdiocese_of_Nidaros \"Archdiocese of Nidaros\"); it then became, and has remained, the seat of the Lutheran [Diocese of Nidaros](./Diocese_of_Nidaros \"Diocese of Nidaros\") and the site of the [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral \"Nidaros Cathedral\"). The city was incorporated in 1838. The current municipality was formed in 1964, when Trondheim merged with [Byneset Municipality](./Byneset_Municipality \"Byneset Municipality\"), [Leinstrand Municipality](./Leinstrand_Municipality \"Leinstrand Municipality\"), [Strinda Municipality](./Strinda_Municipality \"Strinda Municipality\"), and [Tiller Municipality](./Tiller_Municipality \"Tiller Municipality\"), and further expanded on 1 January 2020, when Trondheim merged with [Klæbu Municipality](./Klæbu_Municipality \"Klæbu Municipality\").\\n\\nTrondheim has a mild climate for its northerly latitude, resulting in moderate summers and winters that often remain above the freezing point in seaside areas. At higher elevations, though, the [microclimate](./Microclimate \"Microclimate\") is colder and snowier.\\n\\nThe city functions as the seat of the County Mayor of [Trøndelag](./Trøndelag \"Trøndelag\") county but not as its administrative centre (which is [Steinkjer](./Steinkjer_(town) \"Steinkjer (town)\")). This is designed to avoid making the county administration too [centralized](./Centralized \"Centralized\").\\n\\nTrondheim is home to [football](./Association_football \"Association football\") club [Rosenborg](./Rosenborg_BK \"Rosenborg BK\"), Norway\\'s most successful football club, and [Granåsen Ski Centre](./Granåsen_Ski_Centre \"Granåsen Ski Centre\"), which has hosted the World Championship in [Nordic Skiing](./Nordic_Skiing \"Nordic Skiing\").\\n\\nNames and etymology\\n-------------------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Flag_of_Trondheim.svg/250px-Flag_of_Trondheim.svg.png)](./File:Flag_of_Trondheim.svg)\\n\\nThe [flag of Trondheim](./Flag_of_Trondheim \"Flag of Trondheim\") is one of the few Norwegian municipal flags that is not the banner of arms of the municipal [coat of arms](./Coat_of_arms \"Coat of arms\").\\n\\n\\n\\nSee also: [Names of Trondheim in different languages](./Names_of_Trondheim_in_different_languages \"Names of Trondheim in different languages\")\\n\\nThe city was established in 997 by [Olav Tryggvason](./Olav_Tryggvason \"Olav Tryggvason\") and it was originally named *Nidaros* ([Old Norse](./Old_Norse_language \"Old Norse language\"): *Niðaróss*). The first element of the name was the local river [Nid](./Nidelva \"Nidelva\"). The last element of the name was *[óss](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/óss#Old_Norse \"wikt:óss\")* which meant \"the mouth of a river\". Thus the name meant \"the outlet of the river [Nid](./Nidelva \"Nidelva\")\". Although the formal name was Nidaros, the city was commonly known as *[kaupangr](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/kaupangr#Old_Norse \"wikt:kaupangr\")*, which means \"city\" or \"marketplace\", or more specifically *kaupangr í Þróndheimi* which means \"the city in Trondheim\". Trondheim ([Old Norse](./Old_Norse_language \"Old Norse language\"): *Þróndheimr*) was the historic name for the whole district which is now known as [Trøndelag](./Trøndelag \"Trøndelag\"). This is the area where the people were known as Trønder (*[þróndr](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/þróndr#Old_Norse \"wikt:þróndr\")*). This district name Trondheim meant \"the home of the Trønder people\" (literally \"Trønder-home\") and Trøndelag ([Old Norse](./Old_Norse_language \"Old Norse language\"): *Þrǿndalǫg*) originally meant the \"law area of the Trønder people\" (literally \"Trønder-law\"). The name of the Trønder people derives from the [Old Norse](./Old_Norse \"Old Norse\") word *[þróndr](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/þróndr#Old_Norse \"wikt:þróndr\")* which is an old present participle of the verb *[þróask](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/þróask#Old_Norse \"wikt:þróask\")* which means \"to grow\" or \"to thrive\".[[9]](./Trondheim#cite_note-9)[[10]](./Trondheim#cite_note-10)\\n\\nDuring the late [Middle Ages](./Middle_Ages \"Middle Ages\"), the city name was commonly shortened to **Þróndheimr**, dropping the *kaupanger* part, and over time the name became *Trondhjem*, using the [Dano-Norwegian](./Dano-Norwegian \"Dano-Norwegian\") spelling rather than the [Old Norse](./Old_Norse \"Old Norse\") spelling since the city was part of the Kingdom of [Denmark-Norway](./Denmark-Norway \"Denmark-Norway\") for centuries.\\n\\nOn 21 December 1917, a [royal resolution](./Royal_decree \"Royal decree\") enacted the [1917 Norwegian language reforms](./Norwegian_language_conflict \"Norwegian language conflict\"). Around the time, many municipalities and cities had their names changed to \"Norwegianize\" the spelling and make them look less [Danish](./Danish_language \"Danish language\"). On 1 January 1919, the name of the local [Church of Norway](./Church_of_Norway \"Church of Norway\") diocese was changed from **Trondhjem stift** to **Nidaros bispedømme** (English: [Diocese of Nidaros](./Diocese_of_Nidaros \"Diocese of Nidaros\")).[[11]](./Trondheim#cite_note-11) In 1924, the name of the Norwegian capital city was changed from *Kristiania* to [Oslo](./Oslo \"Oslo\"), removing the name referencing a Danish King in favor of the very old name Oslo. In 1928, a [referendum](./Referendum \"Referendum\") in Trondhjem was held on whether to keep the current name or to bring back the original name of *Nidaros*. The vote resulted in 17,163 votes in favour of *Trondhjem* and only 1,508 votes in favour of Nidaros.[[12]](./Trondheim#cite_note-12) Despite this result, the [Storting](./Storting \"Storting\") voted in 1929 to make some changes. The [Trondhjem Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral \"Nidaros Cathedral\") would be changed to [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral \"Nidaros Cathedral\") effective on 1 July 1929[[13]](./Trondheim#cite_note-13) and the name of the city would change to *Nidaros* starting on 1 January 1930.[[14]](./Trondheim#cite_note-14) This change caused public outrage and even [riots](./Riot \"Riot\") during 1930. This forced the [Storting](./Storting \"Storting\") to reconsider this change. On 6 March 1931, the name was formally changed to *Trondheim*, using the medieval Norwegian spelling instead of the Danish version *Trondhjem*. The name of the diocese and cathedral, however, continued using the name Nidaros.[[15]](./Trondheim#cite_note-15)\\n\\nTrondheim was briefly named **Drontheim** during the [Second World War](./Second_World_War \"Second World War\") as a [German exonym](./German_exonyms \"German exonyms\").\\n\\nHistory\\n-------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Lykkens_Portal%2C_Gamble_Bybro%2C_Trondheim%2C_West_view_20150605_1.jpg/250px-Lykkens_Portal%2C_Gamble_Bybro%2C_Trondheim%2C_West_view_20150605_1.jpg)](./File:Lykkens_Portal,_Gamble_Bybro,_Trondheim,_West_view_20150605_1.jpg)\\n\\nThe [Old Town Bridge](./Old_Town_Bridge \"Old Town Bridge\") of Trondheim\\n\\n\\n\\nFor the ecclesiastical history, see [Archiepiscopate of Nidaros](./Archiepiscopate_of_Nidaros \"Archiepiscopate of Nidaros\").\\n\\nTrondheim was named Kaupangen (English: market place or trading place) by [Viking](./Viking \"Viking\") [King](./King_of_Norway \"King of Norway\") [Olav Tryggvason](./Olav_Tryggvason \"Olav Tryggvason\") in 997 CE.[[16]](./Trondheim#cite_note-16) Shortly after that, it came to be called *[Nidaros](./Nidaros \"Nidaros\")*. Initially, it was frequently used as a military retainer ([Old Norse](./Old_Norse \"Old Norse\"): \"hird\"-man) of King Olav I. It was also frequently used as the king\\'s seat and was Norway\\'s capital until 1217.\\n\\nPeople have lived in the area for thousands of years, as evidenced by the [rock carvings in central Norway](./Rock_carvings_in_Central_Norway \"Rock carvings in Central Norway\"), the [Nøstvet and Lihult cultures](./Nøstvet_and_Lihult_cultures \"Nøstvet and Lihult cultures\"), and the [Corded Ware culture](./Corded_Ware_culture \"Corded Ware culture\"). In ancient times, the [kings of Norway](./List_of_Norwegian_monarchs \"List of Norwegian monarchs\") were hailed in Trondheim at [Øretinget](./Øretinget \"Øretinget\"), the place for the assembly of all free men by the mouth of the River [Nidelva](./Nidelva \"Nidelva\"). [Harald Fairhair](./Harald_Fairhair \"Harald Fairhair\") (865–933) was hailed as the king here, as was his son, [Haakon I](./Haakon_I_of_Norway \"Haakon I of Norway\"), called \\'the Good.\\' The battle of *[Kalvskinnet](./Kalvskinnet \"Kalvskinnet\")* took place in Trondheim in 1179: King [Sverre Sigurdsson](./Sverre_Sigurdsson \"Sverre Sigurdsson\") and his *[Birkebeiner](./Birkebeiner \"Birkebeiner\")* warriors were victorious against [Erling Skakke](./Erling_Skakke \"Erling Skakke\") (a rival to the throne). Some scholars believe that the famous [Lewis chessmen](./Lewis_chessmen \"Lewis chessmen\"), 12th-century chess pieces carved from walrus ivory that were found in the [Hebrides](./Hebrides \"Hebrides\") and are now at the [British Museum](./British_Museum \"British Museum\"), may have been made in Trondheim.[[17]](./Trondheim#cite_note-17)\\n\\nFrom 1152, Trondheim was the seat of the [Archbishop of Nidaros](./Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_Nidaros \"Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Nidaros\") for Norway, which operated from the [Archbishop\\'s Palace](./Archbishop\\'s_Palace,_Trondheim \"Archbishop\\'s Palace, Trondheim\"). Due to the introduction of [Lutheran](./Lutheranism \"Lutheranism\") Protestantism in 1537, the last archbishop, [Olav Engelbrektsson](./Olav_Engelbrektsson \"Olav Engelbrektsson\"), had to flee from the city to the [Netherlands](./Seventeen_Provinces \"Seventeen Provinces\"); he died in what today is [Lier, Belgium](./Lier,_Belgium \"Lier, Belgium\").\\n\\nFrom the 16th through the 19th centuries, the city was repeatedly ravaged by fires that caused widespread damage since many of its buildings were made of wood. The worst occurred in 1598, 1651, 1681, 1708, 1717 (twice), 1742, 1788, 1841 and 1842. The 1651 fire destroyed 90% of all buildings within the city limits. After the \"[Horneman Fire](./1681_Trondheim_fire \"1681 Trondheim fire\")\" in 1681, there was an almost total reconstruction of the city, overseen by General [Johan Caspar von Cicignon](./Johan_Caspar_von_Cicignon \"Johan Caspar von Cicignon\"), originally from [Luxembourg](./Luxembourg \"Luxembourg\"). Broad avenues, such as Munkegata, were created, without regard for private property rights, to limit the damage from future fires. At the time, the city had a population of under 10,000 inhabitants, with most living in the downtown area.[[18]](./Trondheim#cite_note-18)[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nAfter the [Treaty of Roskilde](./Treaty_of_Roskilde \"Treaty of Roskilde\") on 26 February 1658, Trondheim and the rest of [Trøndelag](./Trøndelag \"Trøndelag\") became Swedish territory briefly. [However, after a three-month long siege](./Siege_of_Trondheim \"Siege of Trondheim\"), the area was reconquered 10 months later.[[19]](./Trondheim#cite_note-19) The conflict was finally settled by the [Treaty of Copenhagen](./Treaty_of_Copenhagen_(1660) \"Treaty of Copenhagen (1660)\") on 27 May 1660.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Trondheim_map_1898.jpg/250px-Trondheim_map_1898.jpg)](./File:Trondheim_map_1898.jpg)\\n\\nCity Map of Trondheim in 1898, Norwegian edition\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Plan_of_Trondheim%2C_1942.jpg/250px-Plan_of_Trondheim%2C_1942.jpg)](./File:Plan_of_Trondheim,_1942.jpg)\\n\\nPlan of Trondheim, 1942\\n\\nDuring the [Second World War](./Second_World_War \"Second World War\"), Trondheim was occupied by [Nazi Germany](./Nazi_Germany \"Nazi Germany\") from 9 April 1940, the first day of the [invasion of Norway](./Operation_Weserübung \"Operation Weserübung\"), until the end of the war in Europe, [8 May 1945](./VE_Day \"VE Day\"). The German invasion force consisted of the [German cruiser Admiral Hipper](./German_cruiser_Admiral_Hipper \"German cruiser Admiral Hipper\"), 4 destroyers and 1700 Austrian Mountain troops. Except for a coastal battery that opened fire, there was no resistance to the invasion, which began on 9 April at 5 AM. On 14 and 17 April, British and French forces landed near Trondheim in a failed attempt to liberate Trondheim, as part of the [Namsos Campaign](./Namsos_Campaign \"Namsos Campaign\").[[20]](./Trondheim#cite_note-20) During the occupation, Trondheim was the home of the notorious Norwegian Gestapo agent, [Henry Rinnan](./Henry_Rinnan \"Henry Rinnan\"), who operated from a nearby villa and infiltrated Norwegian resistance groups. The city and its citizens were subjected to harsh treatment by the occupying power, including the imposition of [martial law](./Martial_law_in_Trondheim_in_1942 \"Martial law in Trondheim in 1942\") in October 1942. During this time, the Germans turned the city and its environs into a major base for submarines (which included building the large submarine base and bunker [DORA I](./Dora_I \"Dora I\")), and contemplated a scheme to build a new city for 300,000 inhabitants, *[Nordstern](./Nordstern_(city) \"Nordstern (city)\")* (\"Northern Star\"), centred 15 kilometres (9 miles) southwest of Trondheim, near the wetlands of [Øysand](./Øysand \"Øysand\") on the outskirts of [Melhus](./Melhus_Municipality \"Melhus Municipality\") municipality. This new metropolis was to be accompanied by a massively expanded version of the already existing naval base, which was intended to become the future primary stronghold of the German [Kriegsmarine](./Kriegsmarine \"Kriegsmarine\"). A start was made on this enormous construction project, but it was far from completed when the war ended, and today, there are few physical remains of it.[[21]](./Trondheim#cite_note-21)\\n\\n### Municipal history\\n\\nThe city of Trondheim was established on 1 January 1838 (see [formannskapsdistrikt](./Formannskapsdistrikt \"Formannskapsdistrikt\") law). On 1 January 1864, part of [Strinda Municipality](./Strinda_Municipality \"Strinda Municipality\") (population: 1,229) was amalgamated with Trondheim. Then, on 1 January 1893, another part of Strinda Municipality (population: 4,097) was transferred to Trondheim Municipality. On 1 January 1952, the [Lade](./Lade,_Trondheim \"Lade, Trondheim\") area of Strinda Municipality (population: 2,230) was transferred to Trondheim Municipality. On 1 January 1964, a major municipal merger took place: [Leinstrand Municipality](./Leinstrand_Municipality \"Leinstrand Municipality\") (population: 4,193), [Byneset Municipality](./Byneset_Municipality \"Byneset Municipality\") (population: 2,049), Strinda Municipality (population: 44,600), and [Tiller Municipality](./Tiller_Municipality \"Tiller Municipality\") (population: 3,595) were all merged with the city of Trondheim (population: 56,982), which nearly doubled the population of the municipality.[[22]](./Trondheim#cite_note-22) On 1 January 2020, the neighboring [Klæbu Municipality](./Klæbu_Municipality \"Klæbu Municipality\") (population: 6,050) was merged with Trondheim Municipality.[[23]](./Trondheim#cite_note-23)\\n\\n### Coat of arms and seal\\n\\nSee also: [Flag of Trondheim](./Flag_of_Trondheim \"Flag of Trondheim\")\\n\\nThe [coat of arms](./Coat_of_arms \"Coat of arms\") dates back to the 13th century. To the left, there is an [archbishop](./Archbishop \"Archbishop\") with his staff and [mitre](./Mitre \"Mitre\") in a church archway. On the right, a crowned king holding scales in a castle archway. These two pictures rest on a base which forms an arch. Underneath that arch, are three male heads which symbolise the city\\'s rank as Norway\\'s first capital and the archbishop\\'s place of residence. The scales symbolise justice and the [motif](./Motif_(visual_arts) \"Motif (visual arts)\") is based on the political philosophy of the 13th century, where the balance of power between king and church was an important issue. The three heads at the bottom may symbolise the city council. The motif is unique in Norwegian municipal heraldry, but similar motifs are found in bishopric cities on the continent. The design of the coat-of-arms that was adopted in 1897, and is still used today, was made by Håkon Thorsen.[[24]](./Trondheim#cite_note-24)\\n\\nGeography\\n---------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/13/Nidelva-Trondheim-foliage.JPG/250px-Nidelva-Trondheim-foliage.JPG)](./File:Nidelva-Trondheim-foliage.JPG)\\n\\nAutumn [foliage](./Foliage \"Foliage\") along Nidelva; October 2009\\n\\nTrondheim is situated where the River Nidelva meets [Trondheim Fjord](./Trondheim_Fjord \"Trondheim Fjord\") with an excellent harbour and sheltered condition. In the Middle Ages the river was deep enough to be navigable by most boats. However, in the mid–17th century, an avalanche of mud and stones made it less navigable, and partly ruined the harbour. The municipality\\'s highest elevation is the [Storheia](./Storheia \"Storheia\") hill, 565 metres (1,854\\xa0ft) [above sea level](./Above_mean_sea_level \"Above mean sea level\"). At the summer [solstice](./Solstice \"Solstice\"), the sun rises at 03:00 and sets at 23:40, and then stays just below the horizon. Between 23 May and 19 July, when the sky is cloud-free, it remains light enough at night that no artificial lighting is needed outdoors.[[25]](./Trondheim#cite_note-25) At the winter solstice, the sun rises at 10:01, stays very low above the horizon (at midday its altitude is slightly more than 3 degrees over the horizon), and sets at 14:31.\\n\\n### Climate\\n\\nTrondheim city has an [oceanic climate](./Oceanic_climate \"Oceanic climate\") ([Cfb](./Köppen_climate_classification \"Köppen climate classification\")) or [humid continental climate](./Humid_continental_climate \"Humid continental climate\") (Dfb), depending on the winter threshold used (−3\\xa0°C or 0\\xa0°C). Winters are fairly cold and summers are mild. The part of the municipality further away from the fjord has slightly colder winters, while the part close to the fjord has the mildest winters. Trondheim is mostly sheltered from the strong south and southwesterly winds which can occur along the outer seaboard but is more exposed to northwesterly winds. As with the rest of Norway, the weather is dependent on the weather pattern. High pressure over Central Norway or to the east can last for weeks, while Atlantic Lows from the west also can dominate for weeks. Such stuck opposite weather patterns was evident in 2020, when May saw northwesterlies with cold air even bringing some snowfall, while the following June was warm and sunny. Trondheim experiences moderate snowfall from November to March,[[26]](./Trondheim#cite_note-26) but mixed with mild weather and rainfall. There is often more snow and later snowmelt in suburban areas at a higher elevation, with good skiing conditions in [Bymarka](./Bymarka \"Bymarka\"). All the monthly record lows are from 1955 or older, with half of them from before 1920. The last overnight frost in June was in 1958. The all-time low −26\\xa0°C (−14.8\\xa0°F) was recorded February 1899. The all-time high 35\\xa0°C (95\\xa0°F) was recorded 22 July 1901.\\nThe earliest weather stations were located closer to the city centre, from 1945 onwards the weather station has been located at a higher elevation (Voll, 127 m and Tyholt, 113 m), therefore being slightly colder.\\nA new sunrecorder was established in the city by met.no at [Gløshaugen](./Gløshaugen \"Gløshaugen\") (NTNU campus) December 2015, recording more sunhours than the earlier sunrecorder, which had terrain blocking issues.[[27]](./Trondheim#cite_note-27) There are on average 229 sunhours in July (based 2016–2020).[[28]](./Trondheim#cite_note-28) Trondheim recorded 197 sunhours in October 2016 beating the previous national record for October. In April 2019, Trondheim recorded 308 sunhours, setting a new national record for April.[[29]](./Trondheim#cite_note-29)[[30]](./Trondheim#cite_note-30) In contrast, December 2016 only recorded 10 sunhours.\\n\\nLocated at 63 degrees north, Trondheim experience \"white nights\" with only civil twilight during the height of summer. This light allow for normal daytime activities at night, such as reading a book.\\n\\n| Climate data for Trondheim - Voll 1991–2020 (127 m, avg high/low 2002-2025, extremes 1870–present includes | | | | | | | | | | | | |\\n\\n### Fauna\\n\\nThe city has various wetland [habitats](./Habitat \"Habitat\"). among which there is the *Gaulosen.* The observation tower accommodates for birdwatching and providing information about birdlife.[[34]](./Trondheim#cite_note-34)\\n\\nThough Trondheim is Norway\\'s third largest city, wild animals are regularly seen. [Otters](./European_otter \"European otter\") and [beavers](./European_beaver \"European beaver\") thrive in Nidelva and Bymarka.[[35]](./Trondheim#cite_note-35) [Badgers](./Eurasian_badger \"Eurasian badger\") and [red foxes](./Red_fox \"Red fox\") are not uncommon sights. [Moose](./Moose \"Moose\") and [deer](./Deer \"Deer\") are common in the hills surrounding the city, and might wander into the city, especially in May when the one-year-olds are chased away by their mothers, or in late winter when food grows scarce in the snow-covered higher regions. From 2002 until 2017, a [wolverine](./Wolverine \"Wolverine\") lived in Bymarka.[[36]](./Trondheim#cite_note-36)[[37]](./Trondheim#cite_note-37)\\n\\nCityscape and sites\\n-------------------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/TrondheimFromRoofOfNidarosdomen-improved.jpg/250px-TrondheimFromRoofOfNidarosdomen-improved.jpg)](./File:TrondheimFromRoofOfNidarosdomen-improved.jpg)\\n\\nCentral Trondheim as seen from the tower of the Nidaros Cathedral looking towards [Trondheim Fjord](./Trondheim_Fjord \"Trondheim Fjord\") and [Munkholmen](./Munkholmen \"Munkholmen\") Island\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Torvet_i_Trondheim%2C_2020.jpg/250px-Torvet_i_Trondheim%2C_2020.jpg)](./File:Torvet_i_Trondheim,_2020.jpg)\\n\\nThe city\\'s central square (Torvet) in 2020\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Bakklandet_in_Trondheim_4.jpg/250px-Bakklandet_in_Trondheim_4.jpg)](./File:Bakklandet_in_Trondheim_4.jpg)\\n\\nThe pavement cafes at Bakklandet\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Trondheim-Drone-20160722-009.jpg/250px-Trondheim-Drone-20160722-009.jpg)](./File:Trondheim-Drone-20160722-009.jpg)\\n\\nBakke Bridge\\n\\n[DORA 1](./DORA_1 \"DORA 1\") is a [German submarine](./U-boat \"U-boat\") base that housed the [13th U-boat Flotilla](./13th_U-boat_Flotilla \"13th U-boat Flotilla\") during the Second World War occupation of Norway. Today the bunker houses various archives, among them the city archives, the university and state archives. More recently, DORA has been used as a concert venue.\\n\\n[Kristiansten Fortress](./Kristiansten_Fortress \"Kristiansten Fortress\"), built 1681–1684, is located on a hill east of Trondheim. It repelled the invading [Swedes](./Sweden \"Sweden\") in 1718, but was decommissioned in 1816 by Crown Prince Regent [Charles John](./Charles_XIV_John_of_Sweden \"Charles XIV John of Sweden\").\\n\\nA [statue of Olav Tryggvason](./Olav_Tryggvason_(statue) \"Olav Tryggvason (statue)\"), the founder of Trondheim, is located in the city\\'s central square, mounted on top of an obelisk. The statue base is also a [sun dial](./Sun_dial \"Sun dial\"), but it is calibrated to UTC+1 so that the reading is inaccurate by one hour in the summer.\\n\\nThe islet Munkholmen is a popular tourist attraction and recreation site. The islet has served as a place of execution, a [monastery](./Monastery \"Monastery\"), a [fortress](./Fortress \"Fortress\"), [prison](./Prison \"Prison\"), and a Second World War [anti-aircraft](./Anti-aircraft \"Anti-aircraft\") gun station.\\n\\n[Stiftsgården](./Stiftsgården \"Stiftsgården\") is the royal residence in Trondheim, originally constructed in 1774 by [Cecilie Christine Schøller](./Cecilie_Christine_Schøller \"Cecilie Christine Schøller\"). At 140 rooms constituting 4,000 square metres (43,056\\xa0sq\\xa0ft), it is possibly the largest wooden building in [Northern Europe](./Northern_Europe \"Northern Europe\") and has been used by royals and their guests since 1800.\\n\\nA statue of [Leif Ericson](./Leif_Ericson \"Leif Ericson\") is located at the seaside, close to the old Customs Building, the cruise ship facilities and the new swimming hall. The statue is a replica, the original being located at a Seattle [marina](./Marina \"Marina\").\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Edificios_a_lo_largo_del_r%C3%ADo_Nidelva%2C_Trondheim%2C_Noruega%2C_2019-09-06%2C_DD_46-50_PAN.jpg/960px-Edificios_a_lo_largo_del_r%C3%ADo_Nidelva%2C_Trondheim%2C_Noruega%2C_2019-09-06%2C_DD_46-50_PAN.jpg)](./File:Edificios_a_lo_largo_del_río_Nidelva,_Trondheim,_Noruega,_2019-09-06,_DD_46-50_PAN.jpg)\\n\\nThe [Nidelva](./Nidelva \"Nidelva\") flows through Trondheim with old storehouses flanking both sides of this river. The [Old Town Bridge](./Old_Town_Bridge \"Old Town Bridge\") can be seen on the right side of this panorama.\\n\\n### Shopping\\n\\nMost of Trondheim\\'s city centre is scattered with small speciality shops. However, the city centre\\'s main shopping area is concentrated around the pedestrianised streets *Nordre gate* (English: Northern street), *Olav Tryggvasons gate* and *Thomas Angells gate* even though the rest of the city centre is provided with everything from old, well-established companies to new, hip and trendy shops.\\n\\nIn the mid-to-late 1990s, the area surrounding the old [drydock](./Drydock \"Drydock\") and ship construction buildings of the defunct [Trondhjems mekaniske Værksted](./Trondhjems_mekaniske_Værksted \"Trondhjems mekaniske Værksted\") shipbuilding company at the [Nedre Elvehavn](./Nedre_Elvehavn \"Nedre Elvehavn\") was renovated and old industrial buildings were torn down to make way for condominiums. A shopping centre was also built, known as Solsiden (The Sunny Side). This is a popular residential and shopping area, especially for young people.\\n\\nLarger multi-mall shopping areas are located in the eastern suburb of Lade-Strindheim along the *Haakon VIIs gate* and *Bromstadvegen* streets, and in the southern suburb of Tiller (The latter centred around [City Syd](./City_Syd \"City Syd\")). Swedish store chains are widely present throughout the areas, especially in the DIY and clothing store fields, including [IKEA](./IKEA \"IKEA\"), [Biltema](./Biltema \"Biltema\"), and [Clas Ohlson](./Clas_Ohlson \"Clas Ohlson\").\\n\\n### Nidaros Cathedral\\n\\nThe [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral \"Nidaros Cathedral\") and the Archbishop\\'s Palace are located side by side in the middle of the city centre. The cathedral, built from 1070 on, is the most important [Gothic](./Gothic_architecture \"Gothic architecture\") monument in Norway and was Northern Europe\\'s most important Christian [pilgrimage](./Pilgrimage \"Pilgrimage\") site during the Middle Ages,[[38]](./Trondheim#cite_note-38) with pilgrimage routes leading to it from [Oslo](./Oslo \"Oslo\") in southern Norway and from the [Jämtland](./Jämtland \"Jämtland\") and [Värmland](./Värmland \"Värmland\") regions of Sweden. Today, it is the northernmost medieval cathedral in the world, and the second-largest in [Scandinavia](./Scandinavia \"Scandinavia\").\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Nidaros_cathedral_front.jpg/250px-Nidaros_cathedral_front.jpg)](./File:Nidaros_cathedral_front.jpg)\\n\\nWest front of [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral \"Nidaros Cathedral\")\\n\\nDuring the Middle Ages, and again after independence was restored in 1814, the Nidaros Cathedral was the [coronation](./Coronation \"Coronation\") church of the Norwegian kings. [King Haakon VII](./Haakon_VII_of_Norway \"Haakon VII of Norway\") was the last monarch to be crowned there, in 1906. Starting with [King Olav V](./Olav_V_of_Norway \"Olav V of Norway\") in 1957, coronation was replaced by [consecration](./Consecration \"Consecration\"). In 1991, the present [King Harald V](./Harald_V_of_Norway \"Harald V of Norway\") and [Queen Sonja](./Queen_Sonja_of_Norway \"Queen Sonja of Norway\") were consecrated in the cathedral.[[39]](./Trondheim#cite_note-39) On 24 May 2002, their daughter [Princess Märtha Louise](./Princess_Märtha_Louise_of_Norway \"Princess Märtha Louise of Norway\") married the writer [Ari Behn](./Ari_Behn \"Ari Behn\") in the cathedral.[[40]](./Trondheim#cite_note-40)\\n\\nThe [Pilgrim\\'s Route](./Pilgrim\\'s_Route \"Pilgrim\\'s Route\") (*Pilegrimsleden*) to the site of Saint Olufs\\'s tomb at [Nidaros](./Nidaros \"Nidaros\") Cathedral, has recently been re-instated. Also known as St. Olav\\'s Way, (*Sankt Olavs vei*), the main route, which is approximately 640 kilometres (400\\xa0mi) long, starts in [Oslo](./Oslo \"Oslo\") and heads North, along Lake [Mjøsa](./Mjøsa \"Mjøsa\"), up the valley [Gudbrandsdalen](./Gudbrandsdalen \"Gudbrandsdalen\"), over the mountain range [Dovrefjell](./Dovrefjell \"Dovrefjell\") and down the [Oppdal](./Oppdal_Municipality \"Oppdal Municipality\") valley to end at [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral \"Nidaros Cathedral\") in Trondheim. There is a Pilgrim\\'s Office in Oslo which gives advice to pilgrims and a Pilgrim Centre in Trondheim, under the [aegis](./Aegis \"Aegis\") of the cathedral, which awards certificates to successful [pilgrims](./Pilgrims \"Pilgrims\") upon the completion of their journey.[[41]](./Trondheim#cite_note-41)[[42]](./Trondheim#cite_note-42)\\n\\n### Other churches\\n\\nThe Lutheran [Church of Norway](./Church_of_Norway \"Church of Norway\") has 21 churches within the municipality of Trondheim. They are all a part of the [Diocese of Nidaros](./Diocese_of_Nidaros \"Diocese of Nidaros\"), which is based in Trondheim at the [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral \"Nidaros Cathedral\"). Trondheim](./Territorial_Prelature_of_Trondheim \"Territorial Prelature of Trondheim\"). Being located across the street from the Nidaros Cathedral, the two of them form an unofficial religious quarter along with a [synagogue](./Synagogue \"Synagogue\"), a Baptist church, a [Salvation Army](./Salvation_Army \"Salvation Army\") office, and the 8-auditorium [cinema](./Movie_theater \"Movie theater\") *Prinsen kinosenter*.\\n\\n### Museums\\n\\n[Sverresborg](./Sverresborg \"Sverresborg\"), also named [Zion](./Zion \"Zion\") after [King David](./King_David \"King David\")\\'s castle in [Jerusalem](./Jerusalem \"Jerusalem\"), was a fortification built by [Sverre Sigurdsson](./Sverre_Sigurdsson \"Sverre Sigurdsson\"). It is now an open-air museum, consisting of more than 60 buildings. The castle was originally built in 1182–1183, but did not last for long as it was burned down in 1188. However, the [Sverresaga](./Sverresaga \"Sverresaga\") indicates it had been restored by 1197.[[43]](./Trondheim#cite_note-43)[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nThe Trondheim Science Center ([Norwegian](./Norwegian_language \"Norwegian language\"): *Vitensenteret i Trondheim*) is a scientific hands-on experience center. The [NTNU University Museum](./NTNU_University_Museum \"NTNU University Museum\") (Norwegian: NTNU Vitenskapsmuseet) is part of the [Norwegian University of Science and Technology](./Norwegian_University_of_Science_and_Technology \"Norwegian University of Science and Technology\"). There are also a variety of small history, science and [natural history](./Natural_history \"Natural history\") museums, such as the [Trondheim Maritime Museum](./Trondheim_Maritime_Museum?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Trondheim Maritime Museum\"), the *Armoury*, adjacent to the Archbishops\\'s Palace, Kristiansten Fortress, the music and musical instrument museum [Ringve National Museum](./Ringve_National_Museum \"Ringve National Museum\"), [Ringve Botanical Garden](./Ringve_Botanical_Garden?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Ringve Botanical Garden\"), the [Trondheim Tramway Museum](./Trondheim_Tramway_Museum \"Trondheim Tramway Museum\"), and the [Jewish Museum](./Jewish_Museum_of_Trondheim?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Jewish Museum of Trondheim\"), co-located with the city\\'s synagogue, which is among the northernmost in the world.\\n\\n[Rockheim](./Rockheim \"Rockheim\") ([Norwegian](./Norwegian_language \"Norwegian language\"): *Det nasjonale opplevelsessenteret for pop og rock*, The National Discovery Center for Pop and Rock) opened at the Pier in August 2010. It is located inside an old warehouse, but characterised by an easily recognisable roof in the shape of a box. \"The box\" is decorated by thousands of tiny lights that change in a variety of colours and patterns, and is a landmark in the cityscape – especially on dark winter evenings.\\n\\n### Prison\\n\\nVollan District Jail ([Norwegian](./Norwegian_language \"Norwegian language\"): *Vollan kretsfengsel*) was a [jail](./Jail \"Jail\") during the [nazi occupation of Norway](./Nazi_occupation_of_Norway \"Nazi occupation of Norway\") and was used to imprison both prisoners of war and criminals. Vollan was not considered a [concentration camp](./Concentration_camp \"Concentration camp\").[[44]](./Trondheim#cite_note-NOU1998-44) In a summary of prisoners of war in Norway, numerous prisoners were registered at Vollan. One of its roles was as a [transit camp](./Internment \"Internment\") for [political prisoners](./Political_prisoners \"Political prisoners\"). Many prisoners were taken from Vollan to [Kristiansten Fortress](./Kristiansten_Fortress \"Kristiansten Fortress\") and shot. The prisoners at Vollan were interrogated at the Mission Hotel in Trondheim. Some were also interrogated by [Henry Rinnan](./Henry_Rinnan \"Henry Rinnan\") and his gang.[[44]](./Trondheim#cite_note-NOU1998-44) It was closed in 1971 after the opening of Trondheim Prison at Tunga.\\n\\nTrondheim Prison (Norwegian: *Trondheim fengsel*) is a prison that belongs to the Northern Region of the [Norwegian Correctional Services](./Norwegian_Correctional_Services \"Norwegian Correctional Services\").[[45]](./Trondheim#cite_note-45) The prison can house 184 [inmates](./Inmates \"Inmates\").\\n\\nIt consists of four main departments:\\n\\n* Nermarka (\"Tunga\") – closed department\\n* Detention department (no: *Forvaringsavdelingen*) at Nermarka\\n* Leira – open division. Through joint positive activities, the individual inmate on certain conditions teaches to be responsible with other people.[[46]](./Trondheim#cite_note-46)\\n* division Kongens gt. – halfway house, located in downtown Trondheim.\\n\\n### Attractions\\n\\nThe [water park](./Water_park \"Water park\") and [public pool](./Public_pool \"Public pool\") [Pirbadet](./Pirbadet \"Pirbadet\") is located on the northernmost shore of the Brattøra district, within walking distance of the central station.\\n\\n### Wider urban area\\n\\nTrondheim forms the centre of the [Trondheim Region](./Trondheim_Region \"Trondheim Region\"), and is a common commuting point for work, shopping, and healthcare. Although the official list of [metropolitan regions of Norway](./Metropolitan_regions_of_Norway \"Metropolitan regions of Norway\") defines the region very broadly, the area of two-way commuting where Trondheim residents too would head outwards for transport, shopping, and [upper secondary schools](./Upper_secondary_school \"Upper secondary school\"), consists roughly of Trondheim, [Malvik](./Malvik_Municipality \"Malvik Municipality\"), downtown [Stjørdal](./Stjørdal \"Stjørdal\") (incl. [Værnes](./Værnes \"Værnes\")), downtown [Melhus](./Melhus_Municipality \"Melhus Municipality\"), [Skaun](./Skaun_Municipality \"Skaun Municipality\"), and the lower sections of [Vanvikan](./Vanvikan \"Vanvikan\") in [Indre Fosen](./Indre_Fosen \"Indre Fosen\").[[47]](./Trondheim#cite_note-47)\\n\\nGovernment\\n----------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/R%C3%A5dhuset_i_Trondheim_sett_fra_Bispegata%2C_2023.jpg/250px-R%C3%A5dhuset_i_Trondheim_sett_fra_Bispegata%2C_2023.jpg)](./File:Rådhuset_i_Trondheim_sett_fra_Bispegata,_2023.jpg)\\n\\nTrondheim\\'s town hall.\\n\\nTrondheim Municipality is responsible for [primary education](./Primary_education \"Primary education\") (through 10th grade), outpatient [health services](./Health_care \"Health care\"), [senior citizen](./Old_age \"Old age\") services, [welfare](./Welfare_spending \"Welfare spending\") and other [social services](./Social_work \"Social work\"), [zoning](./Zoning \"Zoning\"), [economic development](./Economic_development \"Economic development\"), and municipal [roads](./Road \"Road\") and utilities. The municipality is governed by a [municipal council](./Municipal_council_(Norway) \"Municipal council (Norway)\") of [directly elected](./Direct_election \"Direct election\") representatives. The [mayor](./Mayor \"Mayor\") is [indirectly elected](./Indirect_election \"Indirect election\") by a vote of the municipal council.[[48]](./Trondheim#cite_note-ks-48) The municipality is under the jurisdiction of the [Trøndelag District Court](./Trøndelag_District_Court \"Trøndelag District Court\") and the [Frostating Court of Appeal](./Frostating_Court_of_Appeal \"Frostating Court of Appeal\").\\n\\nOn 1 January 2005, the city was reorganized from five [boroughs](./Borough \"Borough\") into four, with each of these having separate social services offices.[[49]](./Trondheim#cite_note-49) The current boroughs are [Midtbyen](./Midtbyen,_Trondheim \"Midtbyen, Trondheim\") (44,967 inhabitants), [Østbyen](./Østbyen \"Østbyen\") (42,707 inhabitants), [Lerkendal](./Lerkendal,_Trondheim \"Lerkendal, Trondheim\") (46,603 inhabitants) and [Heimdal](./Heimdal \"Heimdal\") (30,744) inhabitants. The Population statistics listed are as of 1 January 2008. [Prior to 2005](./List_of_boroughs_in_Trondheim_prior_to_2005 \"List of boroughs in Trondheim prior to 2005\"), Trondheim was divided into the boroughs *Sentrum*, *Strinda*, *Nardo*, *Byåsen* and *Heimdal*.\\n\\nSee also: [List of mayors of Trondheim](./List_of_mayors_of_Trondheim \"List of mayors of Trondheim\")\\n\\n### Municipal council\\n\\nThe [city council](./Municipal_council_(Norway) \"Municipal council (Norway)\") *(Bystyret)* of Trondheim Municipality is made up of 67 representatives that are elected to four year terms. Prior to 2011, there were 85 city council members, but this number was reduced to 67 in 2011. Built in 1816, the theatre is the oldest theatre still in use in Scandinavia.[[92]](./Trondheim#cite_note-92) The city also features an alternative theatre house [Teaterhuset Avant Garden](./Teaterhuset_Avant_Garden?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Teaterhuset Avant Garden\"), and the theatre company Teater Fusentast.[[93]](./Trondheim#cite_note-93)\\n\\n### Music\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Ringve_botaniske_hage_1_%2815100598877%29.jpg/250px-Ringve_botaniske_hage_1_%2815100598877%29.jpg)](./File:Ringve_botaniske_hage_1_(15100598877).jpg)\\n\\nThe [Ringve Museum](./Ringve_Museum \"Ringve Museum\") is a museum devoted to music\\n\\nTrondheim has a broad music scene, and is known for its strong communities committed to rock, [jazz](./Jazz \"Jazz\") and [classical music](./European_classical_music \"European classical music\"). The city\\'s interest in Jazz and classical music are spearheaded by the [music conservatory](./Music_conservatory \"Music conservatory\") at [NTNU](./Norwegian_University_of_Science_and_Technology \"Norwegian University of Science and Technology\") which has been called one of the most innovative in the world,[[94]](./Trondheim#cite_note-94) and the municipal music school, *Trondheim Kommunale Musikk- og Kulturskole*.[[95]](./Trondheim#cite_note-95) The [Trondheim Symphony Orchestra](./Trondheim_Symphony_Orchestra \"Trondheim Symphony Orchestra\") and the [Trondheim Soloists](./Trondheim_Soloists \"Trondheim Soloists\") are well-known. The city hosts a yearly Jazz festival, and is home to [Trondheim Jazz Orchestra](./Trondheim_Jazz_Orchestra \"Trondheim Jazz Orchestra\").[[96]](./Trondheim#cite_note-96) The [Fjordgata Records](./Fjordgata_Records \"Fjordgata Records\") label is also hosted in Trondheim.\\n\\nClassical artists hailing from Trondheim include violinist [Arve Tellefsen](./Arve_Tellefsen \"Arve Tellefsen\"), [Elise Båtnes](./Elise_Båtnes \"Elise Båtnes\") and [Marianne Thorsen](./Marianne_Thorsen \"Marianne Thorsen\"). Also the [Nidaros Cathedral Boys\\' Choir](./Nidaros_Cathedral_Boys\\'_Choir \"Nidaros Cathedral Boys\\' Choir\").\\n\\n[Thomas Bergersen](./Thomas_Bergersen \"Thomas Bergersen\"), a Norwegian self-taught composer, multi-instrumentalist, and the co-founder of the production music company Two Steps From Hell, was born in Trondheim.\\n\\nPop/rock artists and bands associated with Trondheim include [Åge Aleksandersen](./Åge_Aleksandersen \"Åge Aleksandersen\"), [Margaret Berger](./Margaret_Berger \"Margaret Berger\"), [DumDum Boys](./DumDum_Boys \"DumDum Boys\"), [Lasse Marhaug](./Lasse_Marhaug \"Lasse Marhaug\"), [Gåte](./Gåte \"Gåte\"), [Keep Of Kalessin](./Keep_Of_Kalessin \"Keep Of Kalessin\"), [Lumsk](./Lumsk \"Lumsk\"), [Motorpsycho](./Motorpsycho_(band) \"Motorpsycho (band)\"), [Kari Rueslåtten](./Kari_Rueslåtten \"Kari Rueslåtten\"), [the 3rd and the Mortal](./The_3rd_and_the_Mortal \"The 3rd and the Mortal\"), [TNT](./TNT_(Norwegian_band) \"TNT (Norwegian band)\"), [Tre Små Kinesere](./Tre_Små_Kinesere \"Tre Små Kinesere\"), [the Kids](./The_Kids_(Norwegian_band) \"The Kids (Norwegian band)\"), [Bokassa](./Bokassa_(band) \"Bokassa (band)\"), Casino Steel (of [the Boys](./The_Boys_(UK_band) \"The Boys (UK band)\")), Atrox, Bloodthorn, Manes, child prodigy [Malin Reitan](./Malin_Reitan \"Malin Reitan\") and [Aleksander With](./Aleksander_With \"Aleksander With\"). The most popular punk scene is [UFFA](./UFFA \"UFFA\").\\n\\n[Georg Kajanus](./Georg_Kajanus \"Georg Kajanus\"), creator of the bands [Eclection](./Eclection \"Eclection\"), [Sailor](./Sailor_(band) \"Sailor (band)\") and [DATA](./DATA_(band) \"DATA (band)\"), was born in Trondheim. The music production team [Stargate](./Stargate_(production_team) \"Stargate (production team)\") started out in Trondheim.\\n\\nTrondheim is also home to Rockheim, the national museum of popular music, which is responsible for collecting, preserving and sharing Norwegian popular music from the 1950s to the present day.[[97]](./Trondheim#cite_note-97)[[98]](./Trondheim#cite_note-98)[[99]](./Trondheim#cite_note-99)\\n\\n### Film\\n\\nTrondheim features a lively film scene, including three filmfests: Minimalen Short Film Fest and [Kosmorama International Film Fest](./Kosmorama \"Kosmorama\") in March, and [Trondheim Documentarfestival](./Trondheim_Documentarfestival?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Trondheim Documentarfestival\") in November. Trondheim has two cinemas in the center of the city, Prinsen Kino and Nova kino [Prinsen Kinosenter](./Prinsen_Kinosenter?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Prinsen Kinosenter\"), [Nova Kinosenter](./Nova_Kinosenter \"Nova Kinosenter\")\\n\\n### Student culture\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Studentersamfundet_i_Trondhjem_from_South-West.jpg/250px-Studentersamfundet_i_Trondhjem_from_South-West.jpg)](./File:Studentersamfundet_i_Trondhjem_from_South-West.jpg)\\n\\nThe building of the [Studentersamfundet i Trondhjem](./Studentersamfundet_i_Trondhjem \"Studentersamfundet i Trondhjem\")\\n\\nWith students comprising almost a fifth of the population, the city of Trondheim is heavily influenced by student culture. Most noticeable is [Studentersamfundet i Trondhjem](./Studentersamfundet_i_Trondhjem \"Studentersamfundet i Trondhjem\"), the city\\'s student society. Its characteristic round, red building from 1929 sits at the head of the bridge crossing the river southwards from the city centre. As the largest university in Norway, the [Norwegian University of Science and Technology](./Norwegian_University_of_Science_and_Technology \"Norwegian University of Science and Technology\") (NTNU) is the host of some 36,000 students.[[100]](./Trondheim#cite_note-100)\\n\\nStudent culture in Trondheim is characterised by a long-standing tradition of volunteer work. The student society is for example run by more than 1,200 volunteers.[[101]](./Trondheim#cite_note-101) [NTNUI](./NTNUI \"NTNUI\"), Norway\\'s largest sports club, is among the other volunteer organisations that dominate student culture in Trondheim. Students in Trondheim are also behind two major Norwegian culture festivals, [UKA](./UKA_(festival) \"UKA (festival)\") and [The International Student Festival in Trondheim](./Isfit \"Isfit\") (ISFiT). NTNU lists over 200 student organisations with registered web pages on its servers alone.[[102]](./Trondheim#cite_note-102)\\n\\n### In popular culture\\n\\nTrondheim culture is parodied on the [Monty Python](./Monty_Python \"Monty Python\") album *[Another Monty Python Record](./Another_Monty_Python_Record \"Another Monty Python Record\")* in the form of the fictitious Trondheim Hammer Dance.[[103]](./Trondheim#cite_note-103)\\n\\nTrondheim is also a key location in the *[Command & Conquer: Tiberian Sun](./Command_&_Conquer:_Tiberian_Sun \"Command & Conquer: Tiberian Sun\")* universe, as it is a critical battleground for both factions.\\n\\nTrondheim was the name of a planet in the Hundred Worlds of the [*Ender\\'s Game* novel series](./Ender\\'s_Game_(novel_series) \"Ender\\'s Game (novel series)\").\\n\\nTrondheim likely serves as an inspiration for the fictional city Tronjheim in [The Inheritance Cycle](./The_Inheritance_Cycle \"The Inheritance Cycle\").\\n\\nSports and recreation\\n---------------------\\n\\n[Granåsen Ski Centre](./Granåsen_Ski_Centre \"Granåsen Ski Centre\"), a [Nordic skiing](./Nordic_skiing \"Nordic skiing\") venue located in Byåsen, regularly hosts World Cup competitions in [ski jumping](./Ski_jumping \"Ski jumping\"), [biathlon](./Biathlon \"Biathlon\") and [cross-country skiing](./Cross-country_skiing_(sport) \"Cross-country skiing (sport)\"), as well as the [1997](./1997_FIS_Nordic_World_Ski_Championships \"1997 FIS Nordic World Ski Championships\") and [2025 FIS Nordic World Ski Championships](./FIS_Nordic_World_Ski_Championships_2025 \"FIS Nordic World Ski Championships 2025\"). Trondheim [attempted but failed](./Trondheim_bid_for_the_2018_Winter_Olympics \"Trondheim bid for the 2018 Winter Olympics\") to become the Norwegian candidate for the [2018 Winter Olympics](./2018_Winter_Olympics \"2018 Winter Olympics\"). Hiking and recreational skiing is available around the city, particularly in [Bymarka](./Bymarka \"Bymarka\"), which can be reached by the tramway. Trondheim Golfklubb, one of the oldest golf clubs in Norway, has a nine-hole golf course in Byåsen. Byneset Golfklubb has a full 18 hole par 72 course, which has hosted the [Norwegian Challenge](./Norwegian_Challenge \"Norwegian Challenge\") of the [Challenge Tour](./Challenge_Tour \"Challenge Tour\") in 2012, as well as a short and easy 9 hole course, located at Spongdal. Klæbu Golfklubb in Klæbu has another 9 hole course, albeit with artificial greens. [Trondheim Airport, Værnes](./Trondheim_Airport,_Værnes \"Trondheim Airport, Værnes\"), situated in [Stjørdal](./Stjørdal \"Stjørdal\") 32 kilometres (20\\xa0mi) away, which is Norway\\'s fourth The domestic route Trondheim – Oslo is among the [busiest air routes](./List_of_busiest_passenger_air_routes \"List of busiest passenger air routes\") in Europe with around 2 million passengers annually.\\n\\nTrondheim boasts the world\\'s only bicycle lift, *[Trampe](./Trampe_bicycle_lift \"Trampe bicycle lift\")*.\\n\\n### Bus\\n\\nThe bus network, operated by [AtB](./AtB \"AtB\"), runs throughout most of the city and its suburbs. A new metro line system went public 3 August 2019. The new transportation system covers the Trondheim area (Trondheim, Malvik, and Melhus). The three metro lines and the city lines that link the city across. The new public transport system becomes flexible, with buses running more often and accommodating more passengers. Fewer travelers must take a detour through the center of Trondheim, but relies more on bus transits.\\n\\nIn addition, the Nattbuss (Night Bus) service ensures cheap and effective transport for those enjoying nightlife in the city centre during the weekends. The Nattbus has other and more expensive prices than ordinary buses.\\n\\n### Boats\\n\\nThe Coastal Express ships ([Hurtigruten](./Hurtigruten \"Hurtigruten\"): Covering the [Bergen](./Bergen \"Bergen\")–[Kirkenes](./Kirkenes \"Kirkenes\") stretch of the coast) call at Trondheim, as do many [cruise ships](./Cruise_ship \"Cruise ship\") during the summer season. Every morning the Hurtigruten ships have one southbound and one northbound arrival and departure in Trondheim.\\n\\nSince 1994 there is also a fast commuter boat service to [Kristiansund](./Kristiansund \"Kristiansund\") (via [Brekstad](./Brekstad \"Brekstad\")), the closest coastal city to the southwest; there is also a second commuter boat service to [Vanvikan](./Vanvikan \"Vanvikan\").\\n\\nA [car ferry route](./Flakk–Rørvik_Ferry \"Flakk–Rørvik Ferry\") from the port of Flakk in the northwest of the municipality, connects Trondheim with [Fosen](./Fosen \"Fosen\").\\n\\n### Rail transport\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Trondheim_tram_2.jpg/250px-Trondheim_tram_2.jpg)](./File:Trondheim_tram_2.jpg)\\n\\nA tram in Trondheim in 2006\\n\\nMajor railway connections are the northbound [Nordland Line](./Nordland_Line \"Nordland Line\"), the eastbound [Meråker Line](./Meråker_Line \"Meråker Line\") to [Åre](./Åre \"Åre\") and [Östersund](./Östersund \"Östersund\") in Sweden, and two southbound connections to Oslo, the [Røros Line](./Røros_Line \"Røros Line\") and [Dovre Line](./Dovre_Line \"Dovre Line\").\\n\\nTrondheim also boasts the northernmost (since closure of [Arkhangelsk](./Arkhangelsk \"Arkhangelsk\") tram in 2004) [tramway](./Tram \"Tram\") line in the world: the [Gråkallen Line](./Gråkallen_Line \"Gråkallen Line\"), the last remaining segment of the [Trondheim Tramway](./Trondheim_Tramway \"Trondheim Tramway\"), is an 8.8 kilometres (5.5\\xa0mi) route (which is mostly single-track outside the innermost parts of the city; except the stretch between Breidablikk and Nordre Hoem stations) which runs from the city centre, through the [Byåsen](./Byåsen \"Byåsen\") district, and up to Lian, in the large recreation area [Bymarka](./Bymarka \"Bymarka\").\\n\\n### Roads\\n\\nNorway\\'s longest road, the [European route E6](./European_route_E6 \"European route E6\") north-south [motorway](./Motorway \"Motorway\"), passes through Trondheim mostly southeast of the major districts, except a long section between Tiller and Sluppen just north of Nidelva. The eastern terminus for [European route E39](./European_route_E39 \"European route E39\") is at Klett narrowly within the municipality border, which heads west to [Møre og Romsdal](./Møre_og_Romsdal \"Møre og Romsdal\").\\n\\nThe later built National Road 706, *Nordre avlastningsvei*, is an alternate bypass that heads northwest instead of northeast at Sluppen, passing through Ila, Piren, and northern Strindheim before rejoining European Route E6 northeast of IKEA. This bypass is slower and has various [roundabout](./Roundabout \"Roundabout\") crosses.\\n\\nVarious bridge projects over the Trondheim Fjord to replace the car ferry have been planned, but none have Status | Automatically protected |\\n| ID | [85130](http://www.kulturminnesok.no/kulturminnesok/kulturminne/?LOK_ID=85130) |\\n|  | |\\n\\n**Nidaros Cathedral** ([Norwegian](./Norwegian_language \"Norwegian language\"): *Nidarosdomen / Nidaros domkirke*) is a [Church of Norway](./Church_of_Norway \"Church of Norway\") [cathedral](./Cathedral \"Cathedral\") located in the city of [Trondheim](./Trondheim \"Trondheim\") in [Trøndelag](./Trøndelag \"Trøndelag\") county. It is built over the burial site of [King Olav II](./Olav_II_of_Norway \"Olav II of Norway\") (c. 995–1030, reigned 1015–1028), who became the [patron saint](./Patron_saint \"Patron saint\") of the nation, and is the traditional location for the consecration of new [Norwegian monarchs](./Norwegian_monarchs \"Norwegian monarchs\"). It was built over a 230-year period, from 1070 to 1300 when it was substantially completed. However additional work, additions and renovations have continued intermittently since then, including a major reconstruction starting in 1869 and completed in 2001.\\n\\nIn 1152, the church was designated as the cathedral for the [Catholic](./Catholic \"Catholic\") Archdiocese of Nidaros. In 1537, during the [Protestant Reformation](./Protestant_Reformation \"Protestant Reformation\"), it became part of the newly established state [Church of Norway](./Church_of_Norway \"Church of Norway\"). It is the northernmost medieval cathedral in the world.[[1]](./Nidaros_Cathedral#cite_note-1)\\n\\nThe cathedral is the main church for the *Nidaros og Vår Frue* [parish](./Parish \"Parish\"), the seat of the [Nidaros domprosti](./Nidaros_domprosti \"Nidaros domprosti\") (arch-[deanery](./Deanery \"Deanery\")), and the seat of the [Bishop](./Bishop \"Bishop\") of the [Diocese of Nidaros](./Diocese_of_Nidaros \"Diocese of Nidaros\"). The [Preses](./Preses_(Church_of_Norway) \"Preses (Church of Norway)\") of the Church of Norway is also based at this cathedral. The church seats about 1,850 people.[[2]](./Nidaros_Cathedral#cite_note-2)[[3]](./Nidaros_Cathedral#cite_note-3)\\n\\nHistory\\n-------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Nidarosdom_1857.jpg/250px-Nidarosdom_1857.jpg)](./File:Nidarosdom_1857.jpg)\\n\\nThe Cathedral in 1857\\n\\nNidaros Cathedral was built beginning in 1070 to memorialize the burial place of [Olav II of Norway](./Olav_II_of_Norway \"Olav II of Norway\"), the king who was killed in 1030 in the [Battle of Stiklestad](./Battle_of_Stiklestad \"Battle of Stiklestad\"). He was canonized as Saint Olav a year later by [Grimketel](./Grimketel \"Grimketel\"), the Bishop of Nidaros (the canonization was later confirmed by the pope[[a]](./Nidaros_Cathedral#cite_note-4)). Around 1070, King [Olav Kyrre](./Olav_Kyrre \"Olav Kyrre\"), who was St. Olav\\'s nephew, began building a large stone church on the site where the wooden church had stood. It was dedicated to the Holy Trinity but was commonly called Kristkirken (an earlier term for cathedral). The altar in this church was to be placed over the grave, and when the church was completed around 1090, St. Olav\\'s shrine was moved here and placed over the altar. In this church, almost all Norwegian royals of the 11th and 12th centuries were buried. Kristkirken was about 50 meters long with a choir, nave, and west tower, and it was the largest church in Norway at the time.\\n\\nNothing of Olav Kyrre\\'s church is visible today. It was gradually replaced by new building parts in the 13th century, but its outline can be seen in the ground plan: as was often the case in the Middle Ages, the later walls were built on the old foundations to save time and costs. During the restoration in the late 19th century, these foundations were excavated and measured, providing some knowledge of the church\\'s architecture.[[4]](./Nidaros_Cathedral#cite_note-5)\\n\\nIt was designated the cathedral of the [Catholic](./Catholic \"Catholic\") [Archdiocese of Nidaros](./Archdiocese_of_Nidaros \"Archdiocese of Nidaros\") from its establishment in 1152 until its abolition in 1537 under the Reformation.[[5]](./Nidaros_Cathedral#cite_note-6)\\n\\nSince the [Reformation](./Protestant_Reformation \"Protestant Reformation\"), it has served as the cathedral of the [Lutheran](./Lutheran \"Lutheran\") bishops of Trondheim (or Nidaros) in the [Diocese of Nidaros](./Diocese_of_Nidaros \"Diocese of Nidaros\"). The architectural style of the cathedral is [Romanesque](./Romanesque_architecture \"Romanesque architecture\") and [Gothic](./Gothic_architecture \"Gothic architecture\"). Historically it has been an important destination for [pilgrims](./Pilgrim \"Pilgrim\") coming from all of [Northern Europe](./Northern_Europe \"Northern Europe\").[[6]](./Nidaros_Cathedral#cite_note-7)\\n\\nIn 1814, this church served as an [election church](./Election_church \"Election church\") ([Norwegian](./Norwegian_language \"Norwegian language\"): *valgkirke*).[[7]](./Nidaros_Cathedral#cite_note-lhw-8) Together with more than 300 other parish churches across Norway, it was a polling station for elections to the 1814 [Norwegian Constituent Assembly](./Norwegian_Constituent_Assembly \"Norwegian Constituent Assembly\") which wrote the [Constitution of Norway](./Constitution_of_Norway \"Constitution of Norway\"). This was Norway\\'s first national elections. Each [church parish](./Prestegjeld \"Prestegjeld\") was a constituency that elected people called \"electors\" who later met together in each county to elect the representatives for the assembly that was to meet in [Eidsvoll](./Eidsvoll \"Eidsvoll\") later that year.[[7]](./Nidaros_Cathedral#cite_note-lhw-8)[[8]](./Nidaros_Cathedral#cite_note-9)\\n\\nAlong with [Vår Frue Church](./Vår_Frue_Church \"Vår Frue Church\"), the cathedral is part of the *Nidaros og Vår Frue* [parish](./Parish \"Parish\") in the [Nidaros](./List_of_churches_in_Trøndelag#Nidaros_domprosti \"List of churches in Trøndelag\") [deanery](./Deanery \"Deanery\") in the [Diocese of Nidaros](./Diocese_of_Nidaros \"Diocese of Nidaros\").[[9]](./Nidaros_Cathedral#cite_note-10)\\n\\nBuilding and restoration\\n------------------------\\n\\nMain article: [Nidaros Cathedral West Front](./Nidaros_Cathedral_West_Front \"Nidaros Cathedral West Front\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Beskrivelse_over_den_tilforn_meget_pr%C3%A6gtige_og_vidtber%C3%B8mte_Dom-Kirke_i_Throndhjem%2C_egentligen_kaldet_Christ-Kirken_-_no-nb_digibok_2010030312001-9.jpg/250px-Beskrivelse_over_den_tilforn_meget_pr%C3%A6gtige_og_vidtber%C3%B8mte_Dom-Kirke_i_Throndhjem%2C_egentligen_kaldet_Christ-Kirken_-_no-nb_digibok_2010030312001-9.jpg)](./File:Beskrivelse_over_den_tilforn_meget_prægtige_og_vidtberømte_Dom-Kirke_i_Throndhjem,_egentligen_kaldet_Christ-Kirken_-_no-nb_digibok_2010030312001-9.jpg)\\n\\nThe church before 1762\\n\\nWork on the cathedral as a memorial to St. Olav started in 1070. It was finished some time around 1300, nearly 150 years after being established as the cathedral of the diocese. The cathedral was badly damaged by fires in 1327 and again in 1531. The [nave](./Nave \"Nave\") was destroyed and was not rebuilt until the restoration in early 1900s.\\n\\nIn 1708, the church burned down completely except for the stone walls. It was struck by lightning in 1719, and was again ravaged by fire. Major rebuilding and restoration of the cathedral started in 1869, initially led by architect [Heinrich Ernst Schirmer](./Heinrich_Ernst_Schirmer \"Heinrich Ernst Schirmer\"), and nearly completed by [Christian Christie](./Christian_Christie \"Christian Christie\"). It was officially completed in 2001. Maintenance of the cathedral is an ongoing process.\\n\\nThe oldest parts of the cathedral consist of the octagon with its surrounding [ambulatory](./Ambulatory \"Ambulatory\"). This was the site of the original high altar, with the reliquary casket of [Saint Olav](./Olav_II_of_Norway \"Olav II of Norway\"), and choir. Design of the octagon may have been inspired by the Corona of [Canterbury Cathedral](./Canterbury_Cathedral \"Canterbury Cathedral\"), although octagonal shrines have a long history in Christian architecture. Similarly, the choir shows English influence, and appears to have been modeled after the Angel Choir of [Lincoln Cathedral](./Lincoln_Cathedral \"Lincoln Cathedral\").\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/Nidaros_domkirke_-_Nidarosdomen%2C_S%C3%B8r-Tr%C3%B8ndelag_-_Riksantikvaren-T324_02_0315.jpg/250px-Nidaros_domkirke_-_Nidarosdomen%2C_S%C3%B8r-Tr%C3%B8ndelag_-_Riksantikvaren-T324_02_0315.jpg)](./File:Nidaros_domkirke_-_Nidarosdomen,_Sør-Trøndelag_-_Riksantikvaren-T324_02_0315.jpg)\\n\\nThe west front in the late 19th century, before restoration\\n\\nIt is joined to the octagon by a stone screen that fills the entire east side of the choir. The principal arch of this screen is subdivided into three subsidiary arches: the central arch frames a statue of [Christ the Teacher](./Christ_the_Teacher \"Christ the Teacher\"), standing on the top of a central arch of three subsidiary arches below him. The space above the principal arch, corresponding to the vault of the choir, contains a [crucifix](./Crucifix \"Crucifix\") by the Norwegian sculptor [Gustav Vigeland](./Gustav_Vigeland \"Gustav Vigeland\"), placed between statues of the [Virgin Mary](./Mary_(mother_of_Jesus) \"Mary (mother of Jesus)\") and the [Apostle John](./John_the_Apostle \"John the Apostle\"). Built into the south side of the ambulatory is a small well. A bucket could be lowered to draw up water drawn from the spring that originated from St. Olav\\'s original burial place. (This was covered over by the construction of later cathedrals).\\n\\nThe present cathedral has two principal altars. At the east end of the chancel in the octagon is an altar at the site of the medieval high altar, behind which stood the silver [reliquary](./Reliquary \"Reliquary\") [casket](./Chasse_(casket) \"Chasse (casket)\") containing the remains of [St. Olav](./Olav_II_of_Norway \"Olav II of Norway\"). This silver-gilt reliquary casket was melted down for coinage by [Christian II](./Christian_II \"Christian II\") and St. Olav\\'s remains buried in an unknown location under the cathedral. The only relic known to have survived is a [femur](./Femur \"Femur\") in a silver-gilt reliquary. Shaped as a forearm, it was given by Queen [Josephine](./Josephine_of_Leuchtenberg \"Josephine of Leuchtenberg\") to St. Olav Catholic Cathedral in Oslo. The original reliquary casket was in the form of a church, with dragon heads on its gables. The dragons are similar to those carved on the gables of Norwegian [stave churches](./Stave_church \"Stave church\"). Surviving medieval reliquary caskets in Norway frequently also bear such dragon heads, for instance, that at [Heddal Stave Church](./Heddal_Stave_Church \"Heddal Stave Church\"). He was the church\\'s and the kingdom\\'s patron saint. The current altar was designed to recall in marble sculpture the essential form of this reliquary casket. It replaces the previous baroque altar, which was transferred to [Vår Frue Church](./Vår_Frue_Church \"Vår Frue Church\").\\n\\nThe second altar is in the crossing, where the transept intersects the nave and the chancel. It bears a large modern silver [crucifix](./Crucifix \"Crucifix\"). It was commissioned and paid for by Norwegian American emigrants in the early twentieth century, and the design was inspired by the memory of a similar silver crucifix in the medieval church. The medieval [chapter house](./Chapter_house \"Chapter house\") may also be used as a chapel for smaller groups of worshipers.\\n\\nAll the stained glass in the cathedral dates from its rebuilding in the 19th and 20th centuries. The windows on the north side of the church depict scenes from the [Old Testament](./Old_Testament \"Old Testament\") against a blue background, while those on the south side of the church depict scenes from the [New Testament](./New_Testament \"New Testament\") against a red background.\\n\\nOrgans\\n------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Nidaros_Cathedral_04.jpg/250px-Nidaros_Cathedral_04.jpg)](./File:Nidaros_Cathedral_04.jpg)\\n\\nNidaros Cathedral Wagner organ\\n\\nTwo [organs](./Pipe_organ \"Pipe organ\") are installed in the cathedral. The main organ was built by the Steinmeyer firm in 1930, and was erected in the north transept.[[10]](./Nidaros_Cathedral#cite_note-11) It then had 125 stops. Installation of the Steinmeyer organ was commissioned in 1930 for the 900th anniversary of the [Battle of Stiklestad](./Battle_of_Stiklestad \"Battle of Stiklestad\"). The organ was funded mostly by donations, particularly by [Elias Anton Cappelen Smith](./Elias_Anton_Cappelen_Smith \"Elias Anton Cappelen Smith\"). In 1962, the organ was heavily rebuilt and moved to the west nave. Many stops were removed; some of them were used to build a new choir organ. This organ was fully restored in 2014.[[11]](./Nidaros_Cathedral#cite_note-12)[[12]](./Nidaros_Cathedral#cite_note-13)\\n\\nThe old Baroque organ built by noted German organ builder [Joachim Wagner](./Joachim_Wagner \"Joachim Wagner\") (1690–1749) during the period 1738–40 was carefully restored by [Jürgen Ahrend](./Jürgen_Ahrend \"Jürgen Ahrend\") between 1993 and 1994. It has 30 stops and is located at a gallery in the north transept.[[13]](./Nidaros_Cathedral#cite_note-14)\\n\\nTourist attraction\\n------------------\\n\\nToday, the cathedral is a popular [tourist attraction](./Tourist_attraction \"Tourist attraction\"). Nidaros Cathedral is the site of the observation of Olav\\'s Wake ([Norwegian](./Norwegian_language \"Norwegian language\"): *Olavsvaka*). This religious and cultural festival is centered upon the anniversary of the death of [Saint Olav](./Saint_Olav \"Saint Olav\") at the [Battle of Stiklestad](./Battle_of_Stiklestad \"Battle of Stiklestad\"). Tourists often follow the historic [Pilgrim\\'s Route](./Pilgrim\\'s_Route \"Pilgrim\\'s Route\") ([Norwegian](./Norwegian_language \"Norwegian language\"): *Pilegrimsleden*) to visit the cathedral for this and other events.\\n\\nAlleged bombing plot\\n--------------------\\n\\nThe cathedral is also familiar to enthusiasts of Norwegian [black metal](./Black_metal \"Black metal\"), as it is featured on the cover artwork of *[De Mysteriis Dom Sathanas](./De_Mysteriis_Dom_Sathanas \"De Mysteriis Dom Sathanas\")*, the 1994 studio album by [Mayhem](./Mayhem_(band) \"Mayhem (band)\"). It was rumored that members of the band who had already been associated with the\\n[burnings of other Christian churches in Norway](./Early_Norwegian_black_metal_scene#Church_arsons_and_attempts \"Early Norwegian black metal scene\") had planned to destroy the cathedral[[14]](./Nidaros_Cathedral#cite_note-onceuponatime-15) in relation to the release of the album. When police arrested former Mayhem bassist [Varg Vikernes](./Varg_Vikernes \"Varg Vikernes\") on 19 August 1993 they had found 150 kilograms (330\\xa0lb) of explosives in his Named after the [homonymous geographical region](./Etymology_of_Norway \"Etymology of Norway\"), Harald\\'s realm was later to be known as the [Kingdom of Norway](./Norway \"Norway\").[[1]](./List_of_monarchs_of_Norway#cite_note-1)\\n\\nTraditionally established in 872 and existing continuously for over 1,100 years, the Kingdom of Norway is one of the oldest states of [Europe](./Europe \"Europe\"): King [Harald V](./Harald_V_of_Norway \"Harald V of Norway\"), who has reigned since 1991, is the 64th monarch according to the official list.[[2]](./List_of_monarchs_of_Norway#cite_note-2) During [interregna](./Interregnum \"Interregnum\"), Norway has been ruled by variously titled regents.\\n\\nSeveral royal [dynasties](./Dynasty \"Dynasty\") have possessed the Throne of the Kingdom of Norway: the more prominent include the [Fairhair dynasty](./Fairhair_dynasty \"Fairhair dynasty\") (872–970), the [House of Sverre](./House_of_Sverre \"House of Sverre\") (1184–1319), the [House of Oldenburg](./House_of_Oldenburg \"House of Oldenburg\") (1450–1481, 1483–1533, 1537–1818, and from 1905), including branches [Holstein-Gottorp](./House_of_Holstein-Gottorp \"House of Holstein-Gottorp\") (1814–1818) and [Glücksburg](./House_of_Glücksburg \"House of Glücksburg\") (from 1905), and the [House of Bernadotte](./House_of_Bernadotte \"House of Bernadotte\") (1818–1905). During the [civil war era](./Civil_war_era_in_Norway \"Civil war era in Norway\") (1130–1240), several [pretenders](./Pretender \"Pretender\") fought each other, and as a consequence, some rulers from this era are not traditionally considered lawful kings and are usually omitted from lists of monarchs. Between 1319 and 1905, Norway was at times part of various unions with neighbouring countries, like The [First Swedish–Norwegian union](./First_Swedish–Norwegian_union \"First Swedish–Norwegian union\"), The [Kalmar Union](./Kalmar_Union \"Kalmar Union\"), [Denmark–Norway](./Denmark–Norway \"Denmark–Norway\"), and [Sweden–Norway](./Union_between_Sweden_and_Norway \"Union between Sweden and Norway\").\\n\\nKings of Norway used many additional titles between 1450 and 1905, such as [King of the Wends](./King_of_the_Wends \"King of the Wends\"), [King of the Goths](./King_of_the_Goths \"King of the Goths\"), [Duke of Schleswig](./Duchy_of_Schleswig \"Duchy of Schleswig\"), [Duke of Holstein](./Duchy_of_Holstein \"Duchy of Holstein\"), [Prince of Rügen](./Principality_of_Rügen \"Principality of Rügen\"), and [Count of Oldenburg](./County_of_Oldenburg \"County of Oldenburg\"). They called themselves *Konge til Norge* (\"King of Norway\"), usually with the style *His Royal Majesty*.[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*] With the introduction of constitutional monarchy in 1814, the traditional style \"[by the Grace of God](./By_the_Grace_of_God \"By the Grace of God\")\" was extended to \"by the Grace of God and the Constitution of the Kingdom\", but was only briefly in use.[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*] The last king to use the *by the grace of God* style was [Haakon VII](./Haakon_VII_of_Norway \"Haakon VII of Norway\"), who died in 1957. The King\\'s title today is formally *Norges Konge* (\"Norway\\'s King\"), with the style \"His Majesty\".\\n\\nKey\\n---\\n\\n*For lists of the prehistoric kings of Norway see [List of legendary kings of Norway](./List_of_legendary_kings_of_Norway \"List of legendary kings of Norway\")*\\n\\n|  |  |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| R | Reign |\\n| I | Independent period |\\n| D | Union with [Denmark](./Denmark \"Denmark\") (1537 – 1814 as [Denmark–Norway](./Denmark–Norway \"Denmark–Norway\")) |\\n| S | Union with [Sweden](./Sweden \"Sweden\") (1814 – 1905 as [Sweden–Norway](./Union_between_Sweden_and_Norway \"Union between Sweden and Norway\")) |\\n| DS | Union with [Denmark](./Denmark \"Denmark\") and [Sweden](./Sweden \"Sweden\") (1397 – 1523 as [Kalmar Union](./Kalmar_Union \"Kalmar Union\")) |\\n| R | *[Interregnum/Regency](./Interregnum \"Interregnum\")* |\\n\\nFairhair dynasty\\n----------------\\n\\nMain article: [Fairhair dynasty](./Fairhair_dynasty \"Fairhair dynasty\")\\n\\nBesides becoming sole king after his father Harold\\'s death, Eric Bloodaxe was king jointly with his father for three years before the latter\\'s death.
